title: The Siberian blast that left no crater 💥
subject: forest
description:
Could a blast like this hit a city today? 👇

On June 30, 1908, the Tunguska event flattened about 800 square miles of Siberian forest and knocked down about 80 million trees. A man 40 miles away was thrown from his chair. Scientists think a space rock about 120 feet wide exploded in the air, so it left no crater; a small comet is an alternative theory. Afterward, an astronomer in Northern Ireland logged a night glow bright enough to read a newspaper after midnight. A Tunguska-type event is expected about once a century on average.

Sources: NASA Science ("The Tunguska Impact, 100 Years Later", via ScienceDaily), Royal Museums Greenwich ("The Tunguska event")

scenes.text: One morning, 80 million trees fell over.
They lay across 800 square miles, all pointing away from one spot.
40 miles away, a man was thrown from his chair. He felt like his shirt was on fire.
It was June 30, 1908, in Siberia. But here's the strange part. There was no crater.
Scientists think a space rock about 120 feet wide exploded miles above the ground.
Soon after, the night sky over Ireland glowed bright enough to read a newspaper after midnight.
